alignment.note: Greek employs the article τῷ with dative ἀνθρώπῳ; Syriac uses the prefixed preposition ܠ with demonstrative ܗܘ plus noun ܓܒܪܐ; Latin uses bare dative homini. All three express the indirect object identically in meaning but through different morphosyntactic strategies.

Greek uses a substantival participial construction (τῷ τὴν ξηρὰν χεῖρα ἔχοντι, 'the one having the withered hand') with double article and accusative object. Latin mirrors this with a participial phrase (habenti manum aridam). Syriac employs a relative clause construction (ܕܝܒܝܫܐ ܐܝܕܗ, 'whose hand [is] withered') with the adjective ܝܒܝܫܐ modifying the possessed noun ܐܝܕܗ, reflecting typical Semitic preference for relative-clause attribution over participial modification.

Vulgate inserts a colon to mark the transition from narrative frame to direct speech. Greek uses a raised dot (·) after the participle ἔχοντι; Peshitta has no overt punctuation marker, relying on syntactic structure alone to signal the speech boundary.

Greek uses the prepositional phrase εἰς τὸ μέσον ('into the midst') with article and accusative neuter adjective. Latin employs in medium, mirroring the Greek structure. Syriac uses the single prepositional phrase ܒܡܨܥܬܐ ('in the middle'), with the preposition ܒ governing the emphatic state noun, a more compact idiomatic rendering semantically equivalent to the Greek-Latin construction.
